title: Skipping work to play Grand Theft Auto VI? You're not alone
summary: Got IT problems at work? Call somebody else. Need to develop some corporate training? It'll have to wait until next week. That's because many video game fans are taking time off to play the…

image.caption: The video game Grand Theft Auto VI is being released on Thursday after a long wait, and many gamers are planning to take time off to play it. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

Got IT problems at work? Call somebody else. Need to develop some corporate training? It'll have to wait until next week. That's because many video game fans are taking time off to play the highly-anticipated Grand Theft Auto VI that comes out Thursday. HR experts say it's far from the first cultural event to have people skipping work.
Fans take time off, call in sick and even buy new gaming systems in anticipation of video game's release
Got IT problems at work? Call somebody else. Need to develop some corporate training? It'll have to wait until next week.

Gabriel Santaguida and Amberley Houseman, a Montreal couple who work as a systems administrator and e-learning specialist, respectively, would normally take care of such things, but they're taking the next two days off work to play the long-awaited video game Grand Theft Auto VI that finally arrives Thursday.
"It actually started as a joke, because Gabriel had said, 'Oh, it would be funny if we took the day off for something like this,'" said Houseman.
"Then I was like, 'Wait, I think I'm picking up what you're putting down.'"
Houseman and Santaguida aren't alone. Many fans are gearing up to play the open-world action adventure video game that lets players commit a wide array of crimes as they explore the fictional world.

Montreal couple Gabriel Santaguida, 28, and Amberley Houseman, 29, who enjoy video games like Stardew Valley, are both taking two days off work to play Grand Theft Auto VI when it's released on Thursday. (Submitted by Gabriel Santaguida)

A survey by U.S. HR company BambooHR polled 1,530 employed adults in the U.S. between Oct. 9-20. It also looked at data from approved and pending paid time off requests filed on their platform by about 575,000 active employees at Canadian companies from 2024 to 2026.

It found that time-off requests were up 13 per cent in the United States and up 6.6 per cent in Canada for Thursday compared to equivalent days last year, though respondents didn't make a direct connection to the game's release.

blocks.text: The survey also found that of those who intended to take time off for an upcoming video game release, 50 per cent were planning to call in sick rather than schedule time off.
Some employers are just giving in.
Grand Theft Auto VI-mania hits Canada

Tech company Logitech is giving its 7,000 employees a paid day off Friday so they can play the game, while game developer Pocket Pair announced a five-day holiday for its gamer employers. Edison Motors, the Canadian electric truck company based out of B.C., announced employees could take the two days off, though they would be unpaid.

"Everybody's got their thing that they're going to take time off for, and for some people it's gaming," said Tara Parry, director of permanent services with human resources consulting firm Robert Half Canada.
"We shouldn't shun them for that, we should find a way to embrace it and get people to be upfront about it."
Why the hype?
Grand Theft Auto VI allows players to control Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval in the fictional U.S. state of Leonida, modelled after Florida.

Like previous iterations of the game, players can steal cars, rob stores and get up to all sorts of other mischief, but it also lets them do simple things such as pet cats and hold hands with their in-game partner.
Gamers get to play as Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval in the fictional U.S. state of Leonida. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)
"This is really a historic franchise. One of the biggest in gaming," said Bradly Shankar, gaming editor at the tech news website MobileSyrup in Mississauga, Ont.

Grand Theft Auto V — which was released on Sept. 17, 2013 — has sold over 235 million copies, according to its publisher Take-Two Interactive, which owns Rockstar Games. At launch it made $800 million US, and just a few days following its release, it hit $1 billion US.
Thirteen years later, Grand Theft Auto VI has already made $1.5 billion US in pre-sales, according to market intelligence firm Sensor Tower.

blocks.text: For Houseman and Santaguida, it wasn't as simple as just pre-ordering the game and clicking download. They had played Grand Theft Auto V on PC, but the new game isn't available on that platform at launch.
"We did actually buy a PlayStation 5 just to play this game. And it's been sitting in the living room ever since," said Santaguida.
With the price of the game and Playstation 5, he estimates it cost about $1,000. But he was able to use credit card points to pay for the gaming system.

Adjusting to the trend
Parry, with Robert Craft Canada, says Grand Theft Auto VI is far from the first major cultural event to have people skipping work or using vacation days.
She says millions of Americans either booked off or called in sick the Monday after the 2026 Superbowl, which she says equated to billions of dollars in lost productivity
"We aren't anticipating that level of impact with Grand Theft Auto, but it does have a meaningful impact."

blocks.text: But, she says businesses could be acknowledging how workers are taking part in these events rather than denying that they're happening.
"Why not embrace it and incorporate it into the corporate environment for Thursday, Friday. Call it what it is, maybe set it up so people are gaming in office as opposed to home alone," she said.

This screenshot shows Brian Heder, a character from Grand Theft Auto VI. Tara Parry says employers should prepare for and embrace cultural events such as the release of the new game. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)
In Canada, Parry says many businesses set up watch parties for employees during the FIFA 2026 World Cup, especially for Canada games.
"Most employers recognize that when Team Canada was playing, productivity was going to grind to a halt. So rather than deny it or fight against it, a lot of companies leaned into it," she said.

blocks.text: While Houseman and Santaguida had to use their own personal days off, they say when they finally sit down to play Grand Theft Auto VI on Thursday morning, it will be a rare chance to preserve some time just for fun.
"When you become an adult with adult responsibilities, then I think the moments to just be a kid are a little more rare. And so we take them where we can get them," said Houseman.
"I think we both know it's a little silly," said Santaguida. "But that's also kind of the fun, right?"
